set.detail:
Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus entered the tribunate on 10 December 134 with formidable connections: grandson of Scipio Africanus through his mother Cornelia, brother-in-law of Scipio Aemilianus, son-in-law of Appius Claudius Pulcher, the princeps senatus. His advisers included the consul of 133, the jurist Publius Mucius Scaevola, and Crassus Mucianus. His brother Gaius later claimed that Tiberius had conceived his programme while travelling through Etruria in 137 and seeing estates worked by imported slaves while free peasants had vanished.

The year moved through escalating confrontations. The agrarian bill was vetoed by the tribune Marcus Octavius; Tiberius responded by suspending public business and sealing the temple of Saturn, then took the unprecedented step of having the assembly depose Octavius. When the Senate refused funds for the land commission, he proposed that the treasure of Attalus III, just bequeathed to Rome, be used to equip new settlers, and that the people rather than the Senate decide the fate of the cities of Pergamon. This invaded the Senate's control of finance and foreign affairs. Finally he stood for re-election to a second consecutive tribunate, which his enemies represented as a bid for tyranny; it was not clearly illegal, but it was without recent precedent.

Our narrative sources are Plutarch's Life and Appian's Civil Wars Book 1, both drawing ultimately on accounts written in the heat of later controversy. Plutarch is sympathetic and personal; Appian frames the year as the beginning of the cycle of civil strife that ended with Augustus, and centres the Italian allies, who he says had most to lose. Cicero, who admired the Gracchi's eloquence but condemned their methods, alternates between praise and blame according to his audience.

Modern scholarship has moved away from seeing Tiberius as either a social revolutionary or a cynical demagogue. The problem he addressed was real, though its nature is debated: Brunt argued for a manpower crisis caused by long overseas service; Rathbone, de Ligt and Rosenstein question whether the free peasantry was declining at all, suggesting instead a problem of under-registration or of a growing population pressing on land. What is not in doubt is the political consequence. By using the assembly against a colleague's veto and against the Senate's prerogatives, Tiberius demonstrated a popularis method that was copied for a century, and his murder introduced lethal violence into Roman politics.
set.debate: Was Tiberius a reformer responding to real rural depopulation (Brunt) or did he exaggerate a manpower crisis (Rich, Historia 1983)? Archaeological survey of the ager Romanus and Etruria does not show the wholesale disappearance of small farms that Appian and Plutarch imply. Whether the crisis Tiberius addressed was demographic decline, under-registration or rural overpopulation remains contested.

set.detail:
The lex Sempronia agraria revived the old limit, traditionally ascribed to the Licinian-Sextian laws of 367, on how much ager publicus any individual could occupy: 500 iugera (about 125 hectares) per head, with an additional 250 for each of up to two sons, so up to 1,000 iugera per family. Land held above the limit was to be surrendered; in compensation, holders received secure, rent-free title to what they kept. The recovered land was to be distributed in small allotments, probably of 30 iugera, which were inalienable and subject to a nominal rent, so that recipients could not simply sell to the rich. A board of three men with judicial power to determine what was public and what private, the tresviri agris iudicandis adsignandis, was elected annually: initially Tiberius, his brother Gaius and his father-in-law Appius Claudius.

The difficulty lay in the land itself. Much ager publicus had been occupied for generations, built on, inherited, mortgaged and sold, and boundaries were rarely recorded. Among the occupiers were wealthy Latins and Italians, who had no vote at Rome and whose access to public land had been tolerated. Appian, who makes the allies central to his narrative, says the rich protested that they would lose ancestral tombs and dowries invested in the land.

The commission survived Tiberius' death and worked actively for several years. Boundary stones (cippi) bearing the names of the commissioners Gaius Gracchus, Appius Claudius and Publius Licinius Crassus, and later of Carbo and Fulvius Flaccus, have been found in Lucania, Campania, Samnium and Apulia. The census figures, 318,823 in 131/130 and 394,736 in 125/124, are often linked to settlement, since allotment raised men into the propertied classes eligible for registration and service, but the inference is fragile. In 129 Scipio Aemilianus had the commission's judicial powers transferred to the consuls, which slowed its work.

A series of later laws, summarised by Appian and partly preserved in the epigraphic lex agraria of 111, dismantled the scheme: first allowing sale of allotments, then halting distribution and converting remaining public land into private property subject to rent, and finally abolishing the rent. By 111 most of Italy's ager publicus had become private land. Whether the Gracchan settlements lasted or simply accelerated the concentration of property is still argued.
set.debate: Whether allies were entitled to allotments and how large the lots were is disputed; the law's text does not survive, and the later lex agraria of 111 (CIL I2 585) is the main documentary witness to its effects. The size of the allotments (30 iugera) is inferred from later evidence; whether allies were eligible for allotments is disputed.

scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

set.detail:
Marcus Octavius was a fellow tribune and, according to Plutarch, a friend of Tiberius Gracchus; he was also a substantial occupier of public land, which Tiberius offered to compensate from his own purse. Octavius' veto blocked the agrarian bill at the concilium plebis. Tiberius first tried to persuade him, then retaliated with an edict suspending the activities of all magistrates and sealing the treasury in the temple of Saturn. When armed supporters of the wealthy appeared and the voting urns were seized, the dispute was referred to the Senate, which offered no solution.

At the next meeting of the assembly Tiberius proposed that a tribune who acted against the interests of the people had ceased to be a tribune, and put a motion to remove Octavius. The thirty-five tribes voted one by one; when seventeen had voted for deposition and one more would make a majority, Tiberius paused and pleaded with Octavius to give way. Octavius refused, the eighteenth tribe voted, and he was dragged from the rostra; his slave who tried to protect him lost his eyes. A client of Tiberius, Quintus Mummius, was elected in his place.

The act had no precedent in the history of the tribunate. Tiberius' defence, recorded by Plutarch, was that the tribune's sacrosanctity derived from the people and could be withdrawn by them, just as the kings had been expelled and Vestal Virgins could be punished. His opponents saw an attack on the veto, the principle of collegiality, and the sacrosanctity of the office, which removed the main constitutional brake on the assembly. Even sympathetic contemporaries were alarmed, and the episode was cited against Tiberius by Scipio Aemilianus and later by Cicero.

Modern historians see the deposition as the decisive escalation of 133. It turned a dispute about land into a dispute about popular sovereignty, the claim that the will of the assembly overrode other constitutional checks. That claim would be revived by Saturninus, Sulpicius, Clodius and Caesar's partisans, while the optimate answer, the senatus consultum ultimum and the right of the Senate to declare emergencies, developed in reaction to it.
set.debate: Whether Octavius' veto was itself an abuse of the tribunate, as Tiberius claimed, is a question already debated in antiquity.

scholarship: Badian, 'Tiberius Gracchus and the beginning of the Roman revolution', ANRW I.1 (1972)

set.detail:
The consular elections of summer 133 coincided with Tiberius' campaign for re-election. Many of his rural supporters were busy with the harvest, and the urban crowd was less reliable. On the day of the tribunician election the assembly met on the Capitol before the temple of Jupiter. Rumours circulated that Tiberius intended to make himself king; when he touched his head to signal that his life was in danger, opponents claimed that he was asking for a diadem.

In the Senate, meeting nearby in the temple of Fides, Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio, the pontifex maximus and Tiberius' cousin, demanded that the consul Scaevola act against the tyrant. Scaevola refused to kill a citizen without trial. Nasica then declared that whoever wished the state to be safe should follow him, drew the hem of his toga over his head in the manner of a priest at sacrifice, and led senators and their attendants to the Capitol. Armed with clubs and the broken legs of benches, they routed Tiberius' supporters. Tiberius stumbled and was clubbed to death, by tradition by the tribune Publius Satureius and Lucius Rufus. Some three hundred others died, and the bodies were thrown into the Tiber; his brother's request to bury him was refused.

The ritual gesture of Nasica has attracted much attention. Linderski argued that the scene was staged as a consecratio, the killing of an enemy of the gods as a sacrificial victim, giving religious sanction to an act without legal basis. The sources disagree on details: Appian stresses the chaos and the Senate's role, Plutarch Nasica's personal leadership. Valerius Maximus and Velleius treat Nasica as a saviour; Cicero alternately praises him as the man who rescued the Republic and admits Tiberius was killed without trial.

The consequences were immediate and long-term. Nasica was sent to Asia on an embassy to escape prosecution and died at Pergamon. A special court under the consuls of 132 punished Tiberius' followers. Above all, as Appian observes, this was the first time since the expulsion of the kings that civil strife had ended in bloodshed at Rome, and it would not be the last.
set.debate: Nasica's acting as pontifex maximus and the religious framing of the killing are interpreted differently; whether he had any legal standing to act is denied by most modern scholars.

scholarship: Linderski, 'The pontiff and the tribune: the death of Tiberius Gracchus', Athenaeum 90 (2002)

set.detail:
Attalus III of Pergamon died in spring 133 leaving his kingdom to the Roman people, while declaring the city of Pergamon itself free. The bequest was challenged at once by Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II, who claimed the throne as Eumenes III, won support among the rural population and slaves he promised to free as citizens of a 'City of the Sun', and defeated and killed the consul Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus in 130. The consul Marcus Perperna captured him at Stratonicea in 129, and he was strangled in prison at Rome.

Manius Aquillius, consul in 129, then spent three years with a commission of ten senators organising the new province. The territory comprised the Attalid heartland: Mysia, Lydia, Ionia, Caria and the Thracian Chersonese. Some territories were detached: Greater Phrygia was granted, or by repute sold, to Mithridates V of Pontus, and Lycaonia went to the sons of Ariarathes V of Cappadocia, killed fighting for Rome. Aquillius built a road network from Pergamon to Side, recorded on milestones that are the earliest Roman milestones in Asia, and was later tried and acquitted for extortion.

The most consequential change came from Gaius Gracchus' law of 123, which established that the tithe and other taxes of Asia would be farmed out by the censors in Rome to companies of publicani for five-year periods. This created a vast source of profit for the equestrian order, and the companies became a powerful lobby. The provincials suffered from their abuses; the exploitation goes far to explain the welcome Mithridates received in 88 and the massacre of Italians known as the Asiatic Vespers.

The province was Rome's richest. Cicero in 66 called it the most fertile land, with tribute exceeding that of all other provinces. A senatus consultum preserved on stone from Adramyttium (the 'SC de agro Pergameno') shows Roman magistrates adjudicating disputes between Pergamon and the publicani over tax-exempt land. Scholars debate whether the annexation was the product of Roman greed or reluctant acceptance of a bequest whose refusal would have created chaos; the five-year delay before organisation suggests the latter.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

set.detail:
Gaius Gracchus, nine years younger than Tiberius, held the tribunate for 123 and was re-elected for 122, a second term now permitted. He was the greatest orator of his generation, pacing the rostra and turning to face the Forum rather than the Senate house, with a slave behind him sounding a pitch pipe to moderate his voice. His programme, carried in a torrent of laws, was far broader than his brother's: he sought to build a coalition of the urban plebs, the rural poor, the equestrian order and eventually the allies.

The legislation, whose chronology is uncertain, included: the lex de capite civis, outlawing capital sentences without the people's authority, which drove Popillius Laenas into exile; the grain law establishing a monthly ration at a fixed low price; the reinstatement of the agrarian commission; the founding of colonies, including Junonia at Carthage, Scolacium and Tarentum (Neptunia); a road-building programme with milestones; the military law; the law on consular provinces; the Asian tax law; and the judiciary law transferring the extortion court to equestrian juries. In 122 his citizenship bill, offering Roman citizenship to Latins and Latin rights to other Italians, was defeated after the consul Gaius Fannius warned the plebs that they would lose their seats at games and festivals.

The Senate's counterattack was subtle. The tribune Marcus Livius Drusus proposed twelve colonies of 3,000 poor citizens each, free of rent, and protection of Latins from flogging, outbidding Gaius without any intention of implementation. Gaius' absence for seventy days in Africa founding Junonia damaged his position, ill omens were reported there, and in the elections for 121 he failed to win a third term.

Ancient judgments were sharply divided. Cicero condemned his grain law as draining the treasury while praising his talent; Plutarch presents him as more passionate and radical than his brother. Modern scholars stress the coherence of his programme and his recognition of the equestrian order as a political force. His judiciary law in particular, according to Varro, made the state 'two-headed', setting senators against equites for half a century.
set.debate: Whether Gaius had a coherent plan to reshape the state (Mommsen) or reacted to events; the chronology of his laws between 123 and 122 is uncertain. The order and dates of the Gracchan laws across 123 and 122 cannot be fixed with confidence.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, 'The lex repetundarum and the political ideas of Gaius Gracchus', JRS 72 (1982)

set.detail:
Gaius Gracchus' grain law obliged the state to sell a monthly ration of wheat to every adult male citizen resident in Rome who applied, at a fixed price of 6 1/3 asses per modius, a little over half the normal market price and, critically, stable regardless of harvest fluctuations. The ration was probably five modii (about 33 kg) a month, enough for one person. To support it, Gaius built public granaries, the horrea Sempronia, near the Tiber, among the first such state storehouses in Rome.

The measure answered a real need. Rome's population was growing rapidly from migration, and grain prices were volatile, especially in years of war or poor harvest in Sicily and Sardinia. A slave revolt in Sicily (135-132) and locust plagues in Africa in 125 had recently disrupted supplies. Gaius' law did not give grain away free, and it was not means-tested: Cicero tells the story of the wealthy consular Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, who had opposed the law, queuing for his ration because, as he said, if Gracchus was going to divide his property among the citizens he wanted his share.

The grain law became the most durable of all Gracchan measures and a permanent fixture of politics. It was modified in a conservative direction by Marcus Octavius (perhaps in the 90s), abolished by Sulla, restored in limited form by the lex Terentia Cassia of 73, extended by Cato in 62 to win the plebs away from Caesar, and made free by Clodius in 58. Caesar cut the rolls from 320,000 to 150,000, and Augustus fixed them at some 200,000. The distribution, the frumentatio, continued into late antiquity, when bread and pork replaced grain.

Ancient conservatives condemned the law as a bribe that emptied the treasury and taught the plebs idleness; Cicero calls it a drain on the aerarium. Modern historians emphasise instead that the regular supply defused famine riots, tied the urban plebs to the state, and created the infrastructure of the annona that sustained the imperial capital.
set.debate: The monthly quantity (five modii) is attested only for later laws and is assumed for Gaius'.

scholarship: Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988)

set.detail:
Gaius Gracchus' judiciary legislation transferred the juries of the permanent extortion court (quaestio de repetundis), established by the lex Calpurnia of 149, from senators to men of equestrian census. The cause was the notorious leniency of senatorial juries toward fellow senators accused of plundering provinces: three governors had recently been acquitted in suspicious circumstances, including Manius Aquillius, organiser of Asia.

A long bronze inscription, found in fragments in the fifteenth century and now in Naples and Vienna, preserves much of an extortion law of this period, usually identified with Gaius' law or with a closely related lex Acilia. It sets out procedure in remarkable detail: a praetor draws up an annual list of 450 jurors, excluding senators and their relatives and requiring a census qualification; prosecutors may be non-citizens; successful non-Roman prosecutors receive Roman citizenship; damages are doubled; and verdicts are by majority vote with a procedure for adjournment (ampliatio). It is the most important surviving Republican statute.

The political effect was enormous. Senators who governed provinces now faced judgment by equites, many of whom were connected with the publicani whose operations governors were supposed to restrain. The danger became clear in 92, when Publius Rutilius Rufus, who as legate in Asia had protected provincials against tax-farmers, was convicted by an equestrian jury and retired to Smyrna. Control of the courts became the central issue between the orders: Caepio's law of 106 tried to share juries, Glaucia's restored equestrian control, Drusus in 91 proposed a mixed scheme, Sulla returned the courts to the Senate in 81, and the lex Aurelia of 70 divided juries among senators, equites and tribuni aerarii.

Whether Gaius consciously sought to elevate the equites as a counterweight to the Senate, or simply to end senatorial collusion, is debated. Either way, the judiciary law is often seen as the moment the equestrian order became a political class.
set.debate: Whether the lex Acilia is Gaius' own law or a colleague's, and whether Plutarch's version (adding equites to the senate) is a confusion with Drusus in 91. Identification of the epigraphic lex repetundarum with Gaius' law or with a lex Acilia is unresolved.

scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

set.detail:
After Gaius Gracchus failed to win a third tribunate, the consul of 121, Lucius Opimius, a bitter enemy who as praetor had destroyed Fregellae in 125, moved to repeal the law founding Junonia. During a sacrifice on the Capitol on the day of the vote, an attendant of the consul, Quintus Antyllius, insulted Gracchan supporters and was stabbed to death. The Senate met the next day, with the body displayed in the Forum, and passed a decree that the consul 'should see to it that the state suffer no harm' (videret ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet).

This formula, later called the senatus consultum ultimum or 'final decree' after Caesar's phrase, had no basis in statute. It authorised nothing specific; it urged the consuls to act and implied that the Senate would back them if they used force against citizens. Opimius summoned senators and equites to appear armed with two slaves each, and recruited Cretan archers. When Gaius and Marcus Fulvius Flaccus occupied the Aventine, he offered an amnesty and then attacked.

The legal status of the decree was contested for the rest of the Republic. Opimius was prosecuted in 120 by the tribune Quintus Decius for killing citizens without trial, defended by the consul Carbo, a former Gracchan, and acquitted on the argument that he had acted under the Senate's authority. Its supporters regarded it as declaring a state of emergency that suspended the citizen's right of appeal; its opponents, invoking Gaius' own lex de capite civis, held that no decree could override a law. The decree was passed again against Saturninus (100), Lepidus (77), Catiline (63), during the disturbances of 52, against Caesar (49), and against Antony (43).

Cicero's execution of the Catilinarian conspirators under the decree in 63 led to his exile in 58, showing that the question was never settled. Modern scholars (Lintott, Ungern-Sternberg, Drogula) generally treat the decree as political rather than legal: it worked only when the consuls had the force and the political support to act.
set.debate: Whether the senatus consultum ultimum gave any legal immunity to magistrates acting under it was disputed in antiquity and remains so.

scholarship: Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1968, 2nd ed. 1999)

set.detail:
Fulvius Flaccus, a former consul and one of the land commissioners, and Gaius Gracchus occupied the Aventine with their supporters on the day after Antyllius' death, invoking the hill's association with the plebeian secessions and the temple of Diana. Fulvius armed his men with Gallic spoils from his triumph; Gaius, according to Plutarch, went unarmed save for a small dagger. They sent Fulvius' younger son, a boy, to negotiate. Opimius detained him and attacked.

Opimius' force, including Cretan archers, stormed the hill. Fulvius was found hiding in a bathhouse and killed with his elder son. Gaius fled across the Tiber by the Sublician bridge, where his friends held off pursuers, and reached the grove of Furrina on the Janiculum, where he was killed by his slave Philocrates at his own request, the slave then killing himself. Opimius had offered his head's weight in gold; one Septimuleius is said to have filled the skull with lead to increase the reward. Some 3,000 of Gaius' supporters were killed then or executed afterward without trial, and their bodies thrown into the Tiber; their widows were forbidden to mourn, and Gaius' widow Licinia lost her dowry.

Opimius then rebuilt the temple of Concord in the Forum, an act seen by many as provocative: someone carved on it at night 'a work of madness makes a temple of concord'. The Senate also built a new basilica, the Basilica Opimia, beside it. Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, withdrew to her villa at Misenum, where she received visitors and spoke of her sons without tears, according to Plutarch. Statues of the brothers were later set up and they were honoured with cult offerings at the places of their deaths.

The deaths of 121 established a pattern: the Senate's decree, armed force, mass executions and a subsequent trial that confirmed impunity. Opimius was acquitted in 120 but convicted in 109 by the Mamilian commission for taking bribes from Jugurtha and died in exile at Dyrrachium. The Gracchi became heroes of the popularis tradition and villains of the optimate one, and both sides of the late Republic defined themselves by their judgment of the brothers.

On the death of Micipsa in 118, Numidia passed jointly to his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal and his adopted nephew Jugurtha, who had won fame and Roman friendships serving under Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia. Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered and defeated Adherbal, who fled to Rome. A senatorial commission under Lucius Opimius divided the kingdom in 116, giving Jugurtha the richer western part, but in 113 he attacked again and besieged Adherbal in his capital Cirta.

Cirta, on its gorge-ringed rock above the Ampsaga (modern Constantine), was a fortress of exceptional strength, and Jugurtha settled for a blockade with siege lines. Inside were many Italian merchants, the negotiatores who had settled in Numidia's trading towns, who organised the defence. Two Roman embassies came; the second, led by the princeps senatus Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, ordered Jugurtha to raise the siege, but he temporised and the envoys left. After some five months the Italians, believing they would be protected by their status, persuaded Adherbal to surrender on the promise of his life. Jugurtha tortured Adherbal to death and massacred all adult males of military age, including the Italians.

The killing of Italian and Roman businessmen caused outrage in Rome, where the tribune Gaius Memmius stoked suspicion that Jugurtha had bought the Senate's indulgence. Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum makes the episode the starting point of his indictment of the nobility's corruption: Rome, he famously has Jugurtha say, was 'a city for sale and doomed to perish if it finds a buyer'. War was declared in 111.

Modern historians caution against Sallust's moralising. Senatorial reluctance may reflect a reasonable desire to avoid a costly war in Africa while the Cimbri threatened the north. But the massacre showed how the interests of Italian traders now shaped Roman foreign policy, as the Asiatic Vespers would do again in 88. Sallust's account, written seventy years later, remains our only detailed narrative.
set.debate: The number of Italians killed is unknown; Sallust's charge of senatorial bribery is generally regarded as tendentious.

scholarship: Kraus, 'Jugurthine disorder', in Kraus (ed.), The Limits of Historiography (1999)
Morstein-Marx, 'The myth of Numidian origins in Sallust', AJPh 122 (2001)

set.detail:
Gaius Marius of Arpinum, a novus homo from an equestrian family with links to the Metelli, had served with distinction at Numantia, held the tribunate in 119, the praetorship in 115 and governed Further Spain. In 109 he went to Africa as legate of Quintus Caecilius Metellus, consul and commander against Jugurtha. When he asked leave in 108 to return to Rome to stand for the consulship, Metellus told him to wait and stand alongside Metellus' young son, then about twenty, which would have meant waiting some twenty years.

Marius stayed, cultivated the equites and Italian traders in Utica by criticising Metellus' slow conduct of the war and promising to capture Jugurtha quickly, and wrote letters home attacking his commander. Sallust says that a soothsayer at Utica told him to trust the gods and to try his fortune. Metellus finally released him only twelve days before the elections; Marius travelled fast and won the consulship for 107 with the support of the equites and the plebs.

The tribune Titus Manlius Mancinus then proposed, and the assembly voted, that the command in Numidia be given to Marius, overriding the Senate's decision to extend Metellus' command. This was a serious breach of convention: the allocation of provinces was the Senate's prerogative. It anticipated the later use of popular legislation to give commands to Pompey (67, 66) and Caesar (59).

Sallust gives Marius a famous speech on taking office, in which he contrasts his own scars and military experience with the nobles' ancestral masks and Greek books, and declares that the nobles despise his newness while he despises their idleness. The speech is a Sallustian composition but captures the new man's resentment and the ideological claim that virtus, not birth, should qualify for command. Marius' election began a career of seven consulships, unmatched in Roman history, and a new style of politics built on military reputation and popular support.

scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)
Carney, A Biography of C. Marius (1961)

set.detail:
Having won the Numidian command, Marius needed reinforcements and found the Senate unwilling to obstruct him, assuming the levy would make him unpopular. Instead, Sallust records, he enrolled volunteers 'not according to the custom of our ancestors, nor from the classes, but whoever wished, mostly the capite censi', those registered only by head because they had property below the minimum qualification for legionary service. This is the most famous and most misunderstood military reform of the Republic.

Its significance lies less in a sudden change than in the culmination of a trend. The property qualification for service had already been lowered, from 11,000 asses perhaps to 4,000 in the second century and to 1,500 by Gaius Gracchus' time, and the state had begun to provide equipment. Marius' volunteers for 107 were probably only a few thousand. But the precedent was decisive. In the following decades armies were increasingly composed of poor volunteers who served for long periods and looked to their general, rather than the state, for a share of booty and for land on discharge, as Marius' veterans received in Africa through Saturninus' law of 103.

The other changes popularly called the 'Marian reforms' are a modern bundle. The cohort of about 480 men as the main tactical unit appears before Marius; the adoption of the eagle as the single legionary standard, ascribed to his second consulship by Pliny; the redesign of the pilum with a wooden rivet to break on impact (Plutarch); and the training of soldiers to carry their own kit, hence 'Marius' mules' (Frontinus, Festus), cannot all be dated or attributed with confidence. The disappearance of the old distinctions between hastati, principes and triarii, and of the citizen cavalry and velites, was gradual.

Modern scholarship (Gabba, Brunt, Gauthier, Cadiou) stresses continuity and argues that the 'proletarian army' of the late Republic was less proletarian than once thought. Yet the link between soldiers and commanders that enabled Sulla's march on Rome in 88 grew directly out of these developments.
set.debate: Gabba saw a decisive proletarianisation; Rich and Cadiou argue the 'Marian reforms' are largely a modern construct, the army changing gradually and recruitment of the poor being neither new nor universal after 107. How far the 'Marian reforms' were Marius' work at all, and how proletarian the late Republican army was, are central debates.

set.detail:
Marius' campaigns of 107-106 took the war to the edges of the Numidian kingdom: he stormed Capsa in the desert, massacring its adult males, and captured a royal treasure fortress on a crag near the Mulucha river, the frontier with Mauretania, when a Ligurian auxiliary found a way up while gathering snails. But Jugurtha remained at large, now allied with his father-in-law Bocchus I of Mauretania, who had joined the war in return for a promise of a third of Numidia.

After two hard-fought battles near Cirta in late 106, in which the Roman army was surprised on the march, Bocchus opened negotiations. Marius' quaestor, the young patrician Lucius Cornelius Sulla, conducted them. In a series of dangerous journeys through Mauretanian territory with a small escort, Sulla persuaded Bocchus that Roman friendship was worth more than his son-in-law. Bocchus wavered between betraying Sulla to Jugurtha and Jugurtha to Sulla. Finally, at a meeting arranged as a peace conference, Jugurtha's companions were cut down and the king handed in chains to Sulla, probably in early 105.

Marius returned to triumph on 1 January 104, when Jugurtha walked before his chariot with his two sons; he was then lowered into the Tullianum, where, according to Plutarch, he remarked on the coldness of 'your bath' and died of starvation within six days. Western Numidia was given to Bocchus, and the rest to Jugurtha's half-brother Gauda.

Sulla made the capture the centre of his own legend. He wore a signet ring showing Bocchus surrendering Jugurtha to him, and in 91 Bocchus set up a gilded group on the Capitol depicting the scene, which nearly caused a riot between Marius and Sulla. Sulla's son Faustus put the image on a denarius in 56. The episode, Plutarch says, was the seed of the enmity between the two men that would end in civil war. Sallust's narrative of Sulla's diplomacy, with a famous character sketch of Sulla, is one of the finest passages of Roman historiography.
set.debate: Whether Jugurtha died in 104 by starvation or strangulation varies between sources.

set.detail:
In 105 two Roman armies were sent to the Rhône valley to stop the Cimbri, Teutones and their allies, who had defeated Roman forces at Noreia (113), in the Rhône valley under Silanus (109) and at Burdigala under Cassius Longinus (107), and had overrun the legate Marcus Aurelius Scaurus, whom they executed after he warned their king Boiorix not to cross the Alps. The proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio, enriched, rumour said, by the gold of Tolosa, and the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus, a new man, commanded perhaps eight to ten legions with auxiliaries.

The two commanders refused to cooperate. Caepio, a patrician, would not serve under Mallius, and camped separately on the opposite side of the Rhône near Arausio (Orange). When Mallius began negotiations with the Cimbri, Caepio, fearing he would receive the credit, attacked alone on 6 October 105. His camp was overrun, and the Cimbri then destroyed Mallius' army, which was trapped against the river. Livy's epitomator and Orosius give 80,000 soldiers and 40,000 camp followers killed; Mallius lost two sons. Only a handful escaped, among them the young Quintus Sertorius, who swam the Rhône in armour.

Granius Licinianus says the Cimbri, fulfilling a vow, destroyed all the booty: gold and silver thrown into the river, horses drowned, armour broken, prisoners hanged from trees. The day was added to the calendar of ill-omened days. Arausio was the worst Roman defeat since Cannae, and the casualty figures, though inflated, reflect a genuine catastrophe for Roman manpower.

The political fallout was immediate. Caepio was stripped of his imperium, the first such deprivation since the kings, and expelled from the Senate; in 103 he was convicted by a court created by the tribune Gaius Norbanus and went into exile at Smyrna. The panic in Rome led to Marius' re-election, in his absence and against the law requiring a ten-year interval, as consul for 104 and every year until 100. Rutilius Rufus, consul of 105, introduced gladiatorial weapons training for the new levies.
set.debate: Numbers of the dead and the exact site on the Rhône are uncertain; Plutarch (Luc 27) supplies the date, 6 October. The figure of 80,000 soldiers killed is widely considered exaggerated; the battle date of 6 October rests on Plutarch, Lucullus 27.

scholarship: Evans, 'Rome's Cimbric Wars (114-101 BC) and their impact on the Iberian peninsula', Acta Classica 48 (2005)

set.detail:
Marius was elected consul for 104 while still in Africa and without standing in person, and was then re-elected for 103, 102, 101 and 100, a run of five consecutive consulships without precedent. The law required a ten-year gap between consulships and personal candidature, and the lex Villia annalis had regularised the cursus. The people suspended these rules because the Cimbri and Teutones, after Arausio, could have descended on Italy at any time, and Marius was the only general who had won a war recently.

The Germans, however, turned away into Spain and northern Gaul in 104-103, giving Marius two years to train his army in southern Gaul. He built camps, dug the Fossa Mariana, imposed hard training and long marches, and promoted able officers including Sulla, who later moved to Catulus' staff. Each re-election required political management at Rome. In 103 his ally the tribune Saturninus helped secure his fourth consulship, and Marius was accused of staging a show of reluctance; in 102 Lucius Appuleius Saturninus again canvassed for him. His colleagues included the patrician Catulus (102), who held the Alpine passes, and Manius Aquillius (101), who suppressed the Second Sicilian Slave War.

After the victories at Aquae Sextiae (102) and Vercellae (101), Marius triumphed jointly with Catulus and was hailed as the third founder of Rome after Romulus and Camillus. His sixth consulship in 100, gained, Plutarch claims, with heavy bribery, ended in the debacle of Saturninus' death, after which he withdrew to Asia and lost political influence for a decade.

The consecutive consulships set a dangerous precedent: in an emergency a single general could monopolise command and office. Later precedents for Pompey's extraordinary commands and sole consulship, and Caesar's dictatorships, were justified in the same way. Sulla's legislation of 81 reinforced the ten-year rule specifically to prevent another Marius.

scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)

set.detail:
In 102 the migrating peoples divided: the Cimbri went round to cross the eastern Alps into Italy, while the Teutones and Ambrones marched toward Italy along the coast through the Roman province. Marius, in a fortified camp on the Rhône, refused to give battle and let his soldiers watch the Germans for days so as to lose their fear. The Teutones, Plutarch says, filed past the camp for six days, mocking the Romans and asking whether they had messages for their wives.

Marius followed them to Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence). A clash between Roman water-carriers and Ambrones bathing in the river escalated into a battle in which the Ligurian auxiliaries and then legionaries destroyed the Ambrones, some 30,000 by Plutarch's figure. Two days later Marius drew up his army on a hill and lured the Teutones into an uphill attack, while his legate Claudius Marcellus, with 3,000 men hidden in woods behind the enemy, attacked their rear at the decisive moment. The Teutonic host was annihilated; the ancient figures, 100,000 to 200,000 killed or captured, are fantastic, but the destruction was complete. Their king Teutobod was captured.

Plutarch, perhaps drawing on Posidonius, records that the people of Massalia fenced their vineyards with the bones of the dead, and that the soil was so enriched by decaying bodies that it gave extraordinary harvests for years. The women of the Teutones, refused their request to be given to the Vestal Virgins as slaves, killed their children and themselves. Marius was preparing to burn the spoils when news arrived of his election to a fifth consulship.

The battle site has been sought near Pourrières, east of Aix, whose name has been derived from campi putridi, 'rotten fields'; the nearby Mont Sainte-Victoire is often linked with the victory. The tactical use of terrain and a concealed reserve shows the quality of Marius' generalship and his trained army.
set.debate: Ancient figures are rhetorical; the precise battlefield is uncertain. Battle site (Pourrières area, Trets, or elsewhere east of Aix) and casualty figures are disputed.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, In the Name of Rome (2003)

set.detail:
While Marius destroyed the Teutones, the Cimbri had crossed the Brenner and driven the consul Catulus back from the Adige in early 102, overrunning the Po plain north of the river during the winter. In 101 Marius, consul for the fifth time, joined Catulus, now proconsul, and the combined army of some 52,000 men (Plutarch: 32,000 under Marius and 20,300 under Catulus) met the Cimbri on the Raudine Plain near Vercellae on 30 July 101. Boiorix, the Cimbric king, rode to the Roman camp to ask for land for his people and that of his brothers the Teutones; Marius replied that the Teutones already had land, which they would hold forever.

The battle was fought in summer heat and dust, which Plutarch says Marius used to his advantage, turning his men so that the sun was in the Cimbri's eyes. The Cimbric infantry, he says, formed a vast square, its front ranks chained together, while 15,000 cavalry tried to draw the Romans away. Marius' wings missed the enemy in the dust, and the decisive fighting fell on Catulus' centre, where Sulla served. Boiorix was killed fighting. The ancient figures, 120,000 to 140,000 killed and 60,000 captured, are inflated but signal annihilation. As at Aquae Sextiae, the Cimbric women killed their children and themselves on the wagon laager.

Credit was bitterly contested. Catulus' soldiers showed the Parmesan envoys that their javelins, inscribed with Catulus' name, were in most of the bodies; Catulus wrote a memoir, and Sulla's memoirs also minimised Marius' role. Plutarch's account, drawing on both, is partisan. Nevertheless the people regarded Marius as the saviour, and the two generals triumphed together. Catulus built the temple of Fortuna Huiusce Diei, probably Temple B in the Largo Argentina, and Marius the temple of Honos and Virtus.

The site of the Campi Raudii is disputed: near Vercelli in Piedmont, as the name suggests, or in the lower Po valley near Rovigo, which some scholars prefer because the Cimbri had come from the Adige.
set.debate: Location (Vercelli versus the lower Po) and numbers are disputed; Plutarch's figures derive from Sulla's hostile memoirs. Location of the Campi Raudii: Vercelli in Piedmont (traditional) or near Rovigo in the Po delta.

set.detail:
Lucius Appuleius Saturninus, tribune for the second time in 100, and the praetor Gaius Servilius Glaucia formed an alliance with Marius, consul for the sixth time, to provide land for his veterans of the German wars. Saturninus' agrarian law distributed land in Transalpine Gaul and founded colonies in Sicily, Achaea and Macedonia, and required every senator to swear within five days to obey the law; Metellus Numidicus alone refused and went into exile. Saturninus also carried a grain law, perhaps lowering the price, and, if the dating is right, the law on praetorian provinces known from inscriptions at Delphi and Cnidus.

The alliance fractured in the autumn. Saturninus was re-elected tribune for 99 and Glaucia sought the consulship, although as a sitting praetor he was ineligible. When Gaius Memmius seemed likely to win the second consular place, he was clubbed to death in the Campus Martius. The Senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum, and Marius, as consul, had to act against his allies. Saturninus, Glaucia and their followers seized the Capitol; Marius cut the water pipes, and they surrendered on a promise of safe conduct. Marius locked them in the Curia Hostilia for their protection, but a crowd climbed onto the roof, tore off the tiles and stoned them to death. Glaucia was dragged from a house and killed.

The episode wrecked Marius' political standing: the optimates mistrusted him and the populares felt betrayed. In 98 Metellus Numidicus was recalled, and Marius left for Asia to avoid witnessing his triumph. Thirty-seven years later the tribune Titus Labienus, prompted by Caesar, prosecuted the elderly senator Gaius Rabirius for Saturninus' murder, a test case on the validity of the senatus consultum ultimum.

Modern scholars differ on Saturninus. Ancient tradition, following optimate sources, depicts him as a violent demagogue; Badian and others see him as a serious legislator with a coherent programme who was destroyed by a collapse of his coalition, and question whether he authorised Memmius' murder.
set.debate: Dating of the Saturnine laws (103 or 100) and Saturninus' responsibility for Memmius' murder are disputed.

sources.r: Lex de provinciis praetoriis (Delphi and Cnidus)

set.detail:
Marcus Livius Drusus, son of the tribune who had outbid Gaius Gracchus in 122, entered the tribunate in December 92 with the backing of leading senators, the orator Lucius Licinius Crassus and the princeps senatus Scaurus among them. His programme was a grand compromise. To restore senatorial control of the courts after the scandalous conviction of Rutilius Rufus, he proposed enrolling 300 equites in the Senate and drawing juries from the enlarged body; to win the plebs he offered colonies in Italy and Sicily and a grain law; and to settle the Italian question he promised citizenship to the allies. To pay for the grain he debased the coinage, mixing one part bronze in eight of silver, according to Pliny.

The first laws passed in the assembly, but opposition grew on all sides. The equites resented losing the courts; many senators distrusted the enlargement; Italian landholders, especially in Etruria and Umbria, feared the agrarian laws; and the consul Lucius Marcius Philippus attacked Drusus relentlessly, declaring in September that he could not govern with this Senate. Crassus answered with his last great speech and died days later. The Senate then annulled Drusus' laws on religious grounds, for having been passed against the auspices and in violation of the lex Caecilia Didia against combining unrelated measures.

An oath of loyalty to Drusus said to have been sworn by Italian leaders, preserved by Diodorus, shows the depth of his connections with the allies; Poppaedius Silo, the Marsic leader, was his guest-friend. Before he could bring the citizenship bill, Drusus was stabbed in the atrium of his house on the Palatine by an unknown assassin, uttering, it was said, 'When will the Republic have another citizen like me?' The allies concluded that Rome would never grant citizenship peacefully, and within weeks Asculum rose.

Ancient writers disagree on whether Drusus was a conservative reformer or an ambitious demagogue; modern scholars generally take him seriously as the last attempt at a negotiated settlement of the Italian question.
set.debate: The authenticity of the 'oath of Philippus' in Diodorus is debated; Mouritsen questions whether the allies wanted citizenship at all, rather than independence.

scholarship: Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)

set.detail:
In late 91 the praetor (or proconsul) Quintus Servilius Caepio learned that hostages were being exchanged among the Italian communities and went to Asculum, the chief town of the Picentes, to investigate. During the Ludi Romani, when he addressed the people in the theatre with threats, the Asculans killed him and his legate Fonteius, then massacred all the Romans in the town and plundered their property. Diodorus preserves a story that a Roman actor and a Latin comic performer were caught up in the violence, the comic surviving by declaring himself no Roman.

The Asculum massacre was the signal for a general rising of the Italian peoples of the central and southern Apennines: the Marsi, Paeligni, Vestini, Marrucini, Picentes and Frentani in the north, and the Samnites, Hirpini, Lucanians, Apulians and others in the south. Latin colonies and most Etruscan and Umbrian communities stayed loyal, as did the Greek cities. The allies sent a final embassy to Rome requesting citizenship; the Senate refused to receive it unless they first laid down arms.

The rising took Rome by surprise despite the warnings, and the first campaigns of 90 went badly. Asculum itself was the last northern stronghold to fall: Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo besieged it through 90 and 89, and inscribed lead sling bullets from the siege, with messages from both sides, survive in their hundreds. When it fell in November 89, the leaders were executed and the rest expelled with nothing.

Appian makes the allies' grievance their exclusion from the rewards of an empire they had helped win, and their exposure to the abuses of Roman magistrates. The massacre fixed the war's character as a ferocious civil conflict fought between men who had served in the same armies. Modern estimates suggest a combined death toll in the war of perhaps 100,000 or more.
set.debate: Whether Caepio was praetor or proconsul, and the exact date in late 91, are uncertain.

scholarship: Dart, The Social War, 91 to 88 BCE (2014)

set.detail:
Having resolved on war, the allies created a state of their own. They chose Corfinium, the Paelignian town in the Aterno valley, as their capital, renamed it Italia, built a forum and senate house there, and set up a senate of 500 members drawn from all the insurgent peoples. Executive power lay with two consuls, the Marsic Quintus Poppaedius Silo and the Samnite Gaius Papius Mutilus, each with six praetors commanding in the northern and southern theatres respectively. The organisation deliberately copied Rome's: they had served in Roman armies for generations and knew its system intimately.

The confederation struck its own coinage on the Roman weight standard, with the legend ITALIA in Latin or VITELIU in Oscan, and images of the bull goring the wolf and of warriors swearing a common oath. The generals' names on the coins (C. PAAPI C., Q. SILO, and others) show the dual language of the alliance: Latin for the northern Marsic group, Oscan for the Samnites. Embassies were sent to Mithridates VI, who was reportedly asked to invade Italy, though he did not.

What the Italians wanted is debated. Appian and Velleius say they fought for the citizenship Rome had refused; the creation of an independent state with its own capital, coinage and magistrates suggests to some modern scholars, especially Mouritsen, that at least some leaders aimed at independence or at the destruction of Rome's hegemony. Others argue that the state was a war organisation designed to force Rome to concede. The Samnites in particular seem to have fought on after others accepted citizenship, and Velleius says Pontius Telesinus in 82 aimed at Rome's destruction.

As northern communities surrendered in 89, the capital moved to Aesernia in Samnium. The confederation dissolved after 88, though Samnite resistance continued and merged with the Marian side in the civil war.
set.debate: Brunt: the allies fought for citizenship. Mouritsen: the citizenship narrative is a retrospective construct and many insurgents sought independence. Whether the confederation sought Roman citizenship or independence is the central interpretive question of the Social War.

scholarship: Pobjoy, 'The first Italia', in Herring and Lomas (eds.), The Emergence of State Identities in Italy (2000)

set.detail:
Late in 90 the consul Lucius Julius Caesar, after a year of defeats and with Etruria and Umbria wavering, carried a law granting Roman citizenship to the Latin communities and to those Italian allies who had remained loyal or who laid down their arms by a fixed date. It was the decisive political concession of the Social War. It was soon followed in 89 by the lex Plautia Papiria, which extended citizenship to individuals of allied communities who registered with a praetor in Rome within sixty days, and the lex Pompeia, which gave Latin rights to the communities north of the Po.

The law also allowed generals to grant citizenship to individual soldiers for valour, as the bronze of Asculum shows Pompeius Strabo doing for Spanish cavalrymen in 89. Communities had to accept the grant by vote; Appian reports that some Greek cities in Italy, such as Neapolis and Heraclea, hesitated because they would lose their treaty rights and institutions. Cicero later discussed the case of Heraclea in defending the poet Archias.

The new citizens were not immediately equal. They were first enrolled in a limited number of new tribes or in eight or ten of the thirty-five existing tribes (sources differ), so that their votes counted for less in the tribal assembly. The distribution of new citizens across all tribes became the political issue that Sulpicius Rufus took up in 88, and that the Cinnan regime implemented in 84. Census registration lagged: the count of 86 showed only 463,000 citizens; that of 70, 910,000.

Velleius noted the paradox that Rome, victorious in the field, granted to the defeated what it had denied to them when they were unbeaten. The law transformed Italy south of the Po into a single citizen body, with the old allied states becoming municipia under their own magistrates, a process of municipalisation that took decades. It created the unified Roman Italy on which the later Republic and the Empire rested.

Proposed by the tribunes Marcus Plautius Silvanus and Gaius Papirius Carbo in 89, this law extended citizenship beyond the communities covered by the lex Julia. Its key clause, preserved in Cicero's Pro Archia, granted citizenship to anyone enrolled as a citizen of an allied community, who had a domicile in Italy at the time of the law, and who registered with a praetor at Rome within sixty days. It thus reached individuals in communities still in arms or whose status was unclear, encouraging defection from the insurgent cause.

Plautius also carried a jury law, the lex Plautia iudiciaria, under which each tribe elected fifteen jurors annually from among senators, equites and even plebeians, ending the equestrian monopoly of the courts. Under this law the Varian court turned on its creators, condemning Quintus Varius himself.

The registration requirement created problems that echoed for decades. The poet Archias of Antioch, enrolled at Heraclea, claimed to have registered with the praetor Quintus Metellus in 89; when he was challenged under the lex Papia of 65, the records of Heraclea had burned in the Social War, and Cicero's speech in his defence depends on witnesses and the praetor's register. The episode shows how administrative the enfranchisement was: a new citizen needed documentary proof and a clerk's entry in Rome.

Combined with the lex Julia and the lex Pompeia on the Transpadanes, the lex Plautia Papiria effectively ended the Social War for most communities. The Samnites and Lucanians, who fought on, received citizenship only from Cinna in 87 or later. The law is a central document in debates over whether citizenship was what the Italians wanted: thousands rushed to register, which suggests it was valued, even if some insurgent leaders aimed higher.
set.debate: The law may have covered only individuals already holding citizenship of federate cities, rather than whole communities; its exact scope is disputed.

scholarship: Badian, 'Roman politics and the Italians (133-91 BC)', Dialoghi di Archeologia 4-5 (1970-71)

set.detail:
In spring or summer 88, from his headquarters at Ephesus, Mithridates VI sent secret letters to the satraps and city magistrates of Asia ordering that on a fixed day, thirty days later, all Romans and Italians in the province, men, women, children and freedmen of Italian birth, be killed, their bodies left unburied, and their property divided between the killers and the king. Slaves who killed their masters were promised freedom, debtors who killed creditors remission of half their debts.

Appian describes the scenes city by city. At Ephesus fugitives were dragged from the temple of Artemis; at Pergamon those clinging to the statues of Asclepius were shot with arrows; at Adramyttium people were driven into the sea and drowned with their children; at Caunus, which owed its freedom from Rhodes to Rome, Italians were torn from the statue of Vesta, their children killed before their eyes; at Tralles the citizens hired a Paphlagonian, Theophilus, to do the killing so as not to stain their own hands, and he cut off the hands of those clinging to statues. Only a few cities, such as Magnesia on the Maeander and Stratonicea, refused, and Rhodes sheltered refugees.

Valerius Maximus and Memnon give 80,000 victims; Plutarch, citing others, 150,000. Both figures are surely exaggerated, but the number of Italian businessmen, tax-farmers, freedmen and their families in Asia was large, and the slaughter was real and thorough. The massacre bound the cities to Mithridates by complicity and secured him huge funds.

The Vespers were the culmination of Asian hatred for Roman tax-farmers and moneylenders, which Mithridates exploited with calculated brutality. Rome's reaction shaped its policy for a generation: Sulla's punitive indemnity of 20,000 talents in 84 and the debts the cities incurred to pay it were still crippling them when Lucullus intervened in 71. Modern scholars debate the role of local class conflict, Greek civic resentment, and royal compulsion.
set.debate: Death toll figures are unverifiable and likely exaggerated. The 80,000 figure is widely regarded as inflated; the date (spring or summer 88) and the degree of local enthusiasm are debated.

set.detail:
Publius Sulpicius Rufus, tribune of 88, was a brilliant orator from the circle of Crassus and Drusus and initially a moderate conservative. In 88 he broke with the optimate leadership, perhaps over the consular candidature of Gaius Julius Caesar Strabo, which he opposed as illegal, and turned to radical legislation, allying with Marius. Plutarch calls him second to none in villainy; Cicero, who heard him as a young man, admired his eloquence.

His laws were: the distribution of the newly enfranchised Italians and of freedmen across all thirty-five tribes, rather than confining them to a few; the recall of those exiled by the Varian court; a ban on senators holding debts of more than 2,000 denarii, aimed at bankrupt nobles; and, most explosively, the transfer of the command against Mithridates from the consul Sulla, who had been allocated it by the Senate and lot, to Marius, then nearly seventy and a private citizen.

To push the laws through, Sulpicius gathered an armed following of 3,000 swordsmen and a 'counter-senate' of 600 young equites. The consuls Sulla and Quintus Pompeius Rufus declared a suspension of public business (iustitium) to prevent voting; Sulpicius' men attacked them, killing Pompeius' son, and Sulla, by one account, took refuge in Marius' house before agreeing to lift the suspension. The laws passed.

Sulla's response, the march on Rome, ended the programme. Sulpicius was betrayed by a slave at Laurentum and killed; his head was displayed on the rostra, and Sulla freed the slave and then had him thrown from the Tarpeian Rock for betraying his master. All Sulpicius' laws were annulled as passed by violence. The question of the new citizens' distribution was revived by Cinna and resolved in 84.
set.debate: What turned Sulpicius from optimate to popularis is disputed; the transfer of the command may have been the price of Marius' support for the tribal law.

set.detail:
Stripped of the Mithridatic command by Sulpicius' law, Sulla went to his army of six legions besieging Nola in Campania, veterans of the Social War who had expected to profit from the eastern campaign. When Marius' military tribunes arrived to take over, the soldiers stoned them to death. Sulla addressed the army and led it on Rome. All but one of his officers, the quaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus, refused to follow, an index of how shocking the act was. Envoys asking why he marched on his country received the reply that he came to free it from tyrants.

His colleague Pompeius Rufus joined him. Marius and Sulpicius, unable to raise forces, offered freedom to slaves who would fight; only three joined. Sulla entered through the Esquiline Gate, fought a street battle in the Forum Esquilinum where his men were pelted from rooftops until he threatened to burn the houses, and took the city. It was the first time a Roman army had captured Rome.

Sulla had Marius, his son, Sulpicius and nine others declared public enemies; Sulpicius was killed, and Marius escaped to Africa after hiding in the marshes of Minturnae. Sulla then passed laws requiring the Senate's prior approval for legislation in the assembly and, according to Appian, voting by the centuriate rather than tribal assembly, and he enrolled 300 new senators. He allowed the election of Cinna as consul for 87 after making him swear to uphold his acts, and then left for Greece.

The march was the decisive breach in Roman political culture. Appian dates the end of shame about civil war to this moment; once an army had been led against Rome, there was no inherent restraint. Sulla's justification, that he acted to restore the legitimate decision of the Senate overturned by violence, would be echoed by Caesar in 49. Modern historians debate whether Sulla planned it or reacted to his soldiers' anger.
set.debate: Whether Sulla's soldiers followed out of greed for eastern plunder (Appian) or genuine belief in the consul's legitimacy is debated. Whether the army's loyalty was to Sulla or to the prospect of eastern booty, and the legality claimed for the march, are discussed by Levick and Morstein-Marx.

scholarship: Levick, 'Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BC', Historia 31 (1982)
Morstein-Marx, 'Consular appeals to the army in 88 and 87', in Beck et al. (eds.), Consuls and Res Publica (2011)

set.detail:
In 87 the consul Lucius Cornelius Cinna revived Sulpicius' proposal to distribute the new citizens across all tribes. His colleague Gnaeus Octavius, backed by the old citizens, drove Cinna's supporters from the Forum in a battle that left, by Plutarch's figure, 10,000 dead. The Senate deposed Cinna, an act without precedent, and replaced him with the flamen Dialis Lucius Cornelius Merula. Cinna went to the army besieging Nola, threw himself on the ground before them, and won them over.

Cinna appealed to the new citizens of Italy, raising money and men, and recalled Marius, who landed in Etruria with a band of Moorish horsemen and freed slaves and enrolled 6,000 men. Sertorius and Gnaeus Papirius Carbo also joined. The armies converged on Rome: Cinna and Carbo on the Tiber south of the city, Sertorius upstream, and Marius seizing Ostia to cut the grain supply. Pompeius Strabo, commanding the only substantial senatorial army, hovered outside the Colline Gate negotiating with both sides, until plague swept through the camps and he died.

The Senate sought help from Metellus Pius, fighting the Samnites, who demanded terms the Senate would not grant; the Samnites themselves came over to Cinna on the promise of citizenship. With Rome starving, the Senate negotiated, asking only that Cinna swear to shed no blood. He refused the oath. Octavius, refusing to flee, sat in his curule chair on the Janiculum and was beheaded; his head was the first consul's head displayed on the rostra.

The siege marked the second capture of Rome by a Roman army within a year. It brought the Cinnan regime to power for four years, during which Cinna held the consulship continuously (87-84), elections were controlled, and Sulla was declared a public enemy while he fought Mithridates in Greece.

scholarship: Lovano, The Age of Cinna: Crucible of Late Republican Rome (2002)

set.detail:
When Marius and Cinna entered Rome in late 87, Marius, bitter from exile and his humiliation in 88, unleashed a five-day massacre. His bodyguard of freed slaves, the Bardyaei, killed whomever he indicated, or whomever he failed to greet. Among the victims were the consul Octavius, the orator Marcus Antonius, betrayed by a wine merchant's indiscretion and killed while charming his executioners with his eloquence, the brothers Lucius Julius Caesar (consul 90) and Gaius Julius Caesar Strabo, Publius Licinius Crassus (father of the triumvir) and his elder son, and Quintus Ancharius, killed while trying to greet Marius. Their heads were displayed on the rostra. Catulus and Merula killed themselves.

The Bardyaei raped and plundered in the houses of their victims until Cinna and Sertorius had them surrounded and killed, some 4,000 by one account, in their camp. Plutarch's narrative, drawing on Sulla's memoirs and other hostile sources, presents Marius as a deranged old man; modern scholars think the killings, though brutal, were more targeted than the sources suggest, aimed at those who had supported Sulla's outlawing of Marius in 88.

Marius and Cinna then appointed themselves consuls for 86 without election. Marius died on 13 January 86, days into his seventh consulship. The young Crassus fled to Spain and hid in a cave for eight months; he would return to fight for Sulla.

The massacres of 87, with heads on the rostra and killings of consulars, set a precedent of political murder that Sulla surpassed in his proscriptions. Their memory kept many nobles loyal to Sulla, whose return in 83 was framed as revenge for these deaths.
set.debate: The number of victims and Marius' personal responsibility versus Cinna's are debated; Plutarch's portrait is heavily coloured by Sullan propaganda.

set.detail:
Marius entered his seventh consulship on 1 January 86, fulfilling, it was said, a childhood omen in which an eagle's nest with seven chicks fell into his lap. His first act was to have the senator Sextus Lucilius thrown from the Tarpeian Rock. He was nearly seventy-one, exhausted by exile and war, and Plutarch says he was tormented by fear of Sulla's return and by sleeplessness, drinking heavily. He fell ill with pleurisy and died on 13 January after seventeen days in office.

Posidonius, who was in Rome on an embassy from Rhodes and met him on his sickbed, is cited by Plutarch as the source for his final days, in which Marius was delirious and imagined himself fighting Mithridates. Livy says he had done more harm in peace than good in war.

Marius' career encapsulates the late Republic: the new man who became the greatest general of his age, saviour of Italy from the Germans, seven times consul, yet politically clumsy and ultimately destructive. His military innovations, real or attributed, created armies personally loyal to their generals; his alliance with tribunes against the Senate made the popularis method a vehicle for military power. His enmity with Sulla, born in Numidia, led directly to the civil wars.

After his victory in 82, Sulla had Marius' ashes dug up and scattered in the Anio and his monuments destroyed. His nephew by marriage, Julius Caesar, restored the trophies of his victories to the Capitol by night as aedile in 65 and displayed his images at his aunt Julia's funeral in 69, signalling that the Marian cause lived on. His adopted son, Gaius Marius the Younger, became consul in 82 at about twenty-six and died at Praeneste.

scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)

set.detail:
Sulla landed in Epirus in spring 87 with five legions and marched directly on Athens, which under Aristion had joined Mithridates, and on the Piraeus, held by the Pontic general Archelaus. He besieged both through the winter of 87/86. To build siege works he cut down the groves of the Academy and the Lyceum; to pay his army, cut off from Rome where his enemies now ruled, he took the treasures of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus.

The Piraeus, protected by the Long Walls and Themistocles' fortifications, was resupplied by sea; the Pontic and Roman engineers fought a duel of mines and countermines, and Archelaus' sorties burned Sulla's engines. Athens itself starved. Plutarch reports a medimnus of wheat selling for 1,000 drachmas, people eating boiled shoes and leather flasks, while Aristion feasted and mocked Sulla and his wife Metella from the walls. Sulla's spies discovered an unguarded section of wall near the Heptachalcon, between the Piraeus and Sacred Gates, and on the night of 1 March 86 his men broke in.

The sack was savage. Plutarch, citing eyewitnesses, says blood flowed through the Ceramicus out of the Dipylon gate; the number killed was never counted. Sulla stopped the slaughter, he said, sparing the living for the sake of the dead, in deference to Athens' past. Aristion held out on the Acropolis until thirst forced surrender and was executed. Sulla then stormed the Piraeus, burning the arsenal of Philo, and Archelaus withdrew by sea.

Archaeologists have found the destruction layer across the Agora and Ceramicus and thousands of sling bullets. Sulla took to Rome the library of Apellicon of Teos, containing manuscripts of Aristotle and Theophrastus that later formed the basis of Andronicus of Rhodes' edition of Aristotle.
set.debate: Date of the fall (1 March 86, the Kalends) rests on Plutarch citing Sulla's memoirs.

scholarship: Habicht, Athens from Alexander to Antony (1997)

set.detail:
After the fall of Athens, Archelaus joined the Pontic army that had come down through Thessaly under Taxiles, giving a combined force that Plutarch and Appian put at 120,000 men, including scythed chariots, phalanx infantry with bronze shields, and freed slaves. Sulla had some 16,500 Romans plus Greek allies. He took up a position in western Boeotia near Chaeronea, scene of Philip II's victory in 338, and kept his men digging trenches to deny the Pontic cavalry room and to keep them from idleness.

Two men of Chaeronea guided a Roman detachment around Mount Thurium, from which they dislodged a Pontic force that fled down onto its own army. The Pontic chariots, launched without room to gather speed, were driven back by Roman javelins and stakes planted in front of the legions, to the derisive applause of the Roman soldiers, who called for more as at the circus. The Pontic phalanx, interspersed with freed slaves, was attacked from the flanks by Sulla's cavalry and by Murena and Hortensius. The rout drove the Pontic army against the hills; Archelaus escaped to Chalcis with 10,000 men.

Sulla claimed that only fourteen Romans were missing, and two of those turned up the next day, figures that surely come from his own memoirs. He set up two trophies, one on the plain and one on Mount Thurium, recording the names of Ares, Nike and Aphrodite, and his cognomen Epaphroditus. The base of the Thurium trophy was found in 1990, with an inscription naming the two Chaeroneans, Homoloichos and Anaxidamos.

Chaeronea, together with Orchomenus later that year, destroyed Mithridates' armies in Greece. Plutarch, himself a native of Chaeronea, describes local memories and finds of armour and weapons in the marshes generations later.
set.debate: Sulla's casualty figures are self-glorifying; Pontic numbers vary widely. Pontic numbers and the near-zero Roman losses come from Sulla's memoirs and are not credible as given.

scholarship: Camp et al., 'A trophy from the battle of Chaironeia of 86 B.C.', AJA 96 (1992)

set.detail:
By 85 Mithridates had lost two armies in Greece, faced revolts in Asia, and was pursued by Fimbria, who had murdered the consul Flaccus and taken command of the Valerian legions. Sulla, for his part, needed to return to Italy to deal with his enemies. Negotiations began through Archelaus at Delium in the winter of 86/85, and Sulla crossed to Asia. In August 85 he met Mithridates at Dardanus in the Troad.

Plutarch describes the encounter: Mithridates came with 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and a fleet; Sulla with four cohorts and 200 horsemen. When the king held out his hand, Sulla demanded whether he accepted the terms, and when Mithridates tried to justify his actions, Sulla cut him off. The terms: Mithridates was to evacuate all his conquests and return to the borders of Pontus as before the war; surrender seventy (or eighty) warships with crews and 500 archers; pay an indemnity of 2,000 or 3,000 talents; release prisoners and deserters; and restore Nicomedes IV to Bithynia and Ariobarzanes to Cappadocia. In return Mithridates was recognised as a friend and ally of Rome and kept his kingdom.

Sulla's soldiers were angry, believing they had been cheated of the king who had massacred 80,000 Italians. Sulla's answer was that he could not fight Mithridates and Fimbria at once. He then marched on Fimbria, whose army deserted.

The treaty was never ratified by the Senate, and its informal status allowed Murena to provoke the Second Mithridatic War in 83. Mithridates lost nothing of his own kingdom and rebuilt his forces for the third war in 74. Modern scholars regard the peace as a pragmatic decision that sacrificed Rome's long-term interest in the East to Sulla's political needs at home, which is broadly how Mithridates' enemies saw it at the time.
set.debate: The indemnity (2,000 or 3,000 talents) and the number of ships vary in the sources.

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

set.detail:
In spring 83 Sulla crossed from Dyrrachium to Brundisium with some 1,600 ships carrying perhaps 40,000 men: five legions of veterans, 6,000 cavalry and contingents from Macedonia and the Peloponnese. Before sailing, the soldiers swore to remain with him and not to plunder Italy, and offered him their own savings. Brundisium opened its gates without resistance, and Sulla rewarded it with an exemption from customs duties that it still held in Appian's day.

Sulla had written to the Senate in 84 listing his services and announcing that he would punish his enemies but not harm the new citizens, a crucial reassurance to Italy. The Cinnan government had prepared perhaps 100,000 men under the consuls of 83, Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and Gaius Norbanus, and Carbo. But its legitimacy had collapsed with Cinna's murder by his own troops at Ancona in 84, and many nobles came over to Sulla: Metellus Pius from Africa, Marcus Crassus from Spain, the young Pompey with three legions raised in Picenum, Cethegus, Verres and others.

Sulla marched up the Via Appia. Near Canusium or at Mount Tifata outside Capua he defeated Norbanus, who withdrew to Capua; at Teanum the army of Scipio went over to him during a truce. Sertorius, who had warned against negotiation, left for Spain. A severe winter halted operations. In July the Capitoline temple burned down, a portent that both sides interpreted in their favour.

The landing opened the Second Sullan Civil War, fought across Italy through 83 and 82 and ending at the Colline Gate. Its outcome depended less on battles than on defections. Sulla later claimed in his memoirs that favourable omens and the support of the gods had accompanied every step, building his image as Felix, the fortunate.

In autumn 82, with the younger Marius besieged in Praeneste and Carbo's armies in the north collapsing, the Samnite leader Pontius Telesinus and the Lucanian Marcus Lamponius, together with the remnants of the Marian forces under Carrinas and Censorinus, broke away from the attempt to relieve Praeneste and marched on Rome itself, which was virtually undefended. Velleius records Telesinus riding along his lines declaring that the wolves who had ravaged Italy's liberty would never disappear until the forest that sheltered them was cut down: Rome must be destroyed.

Sulla raced back and arrived at midday on 1 November 82 outside the Colline Gate, at the north-east of the city, where Telesinus had camped. Against the advice of his officers, he attacked late in the afternoon with tired troops. His left wing, under his personal command, was broken and driven back against the city walls; the gates were shut on the fugitives, and Sulla himself narrowly escaped javelins, praying, it was said, to a small golden image of Apollo from Delphi he carried. On the right, however, Crassus routed the enemy and pursued them to Antemnae. The battle continued into the night.

Over 50,000 men are said to have died on both sides. The next day 3,000 to 8,000 prisoners, mostly Samnites, were herded into the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius and massacred while Sulla addressed the Senate in the nearby temple of Bellona; when the senators flinched at the screams, he told them to pay attention, it was only some criminals being punished. Telesinus' head was paraded before Praeneste, whose garrison surrendered; Marius the Younger killed himself.

Sulla then devastated Samnium, declaring that no Roman would be safe while the Samnites existed. Strabo, writing under Augustus, says that their towns had become villages. The battle ended the civil war in Italy, opened the proscriptions, and was later commemorated by Sulla's Ludi Victoriae.
set.debate: Numbers of prisoners massacred in the Villa Publica range from 3,000 (Livy) to 8,000 (Plutarch).

set.detail:
In November 82 Sulla posted a list (proscriptio, a public notice) in the Forum of men declared outlaws: anyone could kill them, their killers received two talents (12,000 denarii) from the treasury, informers received rewards, slaves who killed their masters were freed, and those who sheltered the proscribed were themselves put to death. The property of the proscribed was confiscated and sold at auction; their sons and grandsons were barred from public office.

The first list had eighty names; others followed, and the lists were closed only on 1 June 81 under the lex Cornelia de proscriptione. Estimates of the dead vary: 40 senators and 1,600 equites in Appian's first phase, 4,700 in all according to Valerius Maximus. Many more died outside Rome as local enemies settled scores. Plutarch reports the remark that a man was killed for his Alban villa, and that the young senator Gaius Metellus asked in the Senate when the killing would end, at least telling the living who was safe.

The proscriptions were also a vast transfer of property. Sulla's freedman Chrysogonus bought the estates of the murdered Sextus Roscius of Ameria, worth six million sesterces, for 2,000; Cicero exposed the case in 80. Crassus built his fortune by buying confiscated estates cheaply, and Catiline was later accused of murdering his own brother-in-law and having him added to the list. The young Caesar, Cinna's son-in-law, was threatened and went into hiding.

The proscriptions were remembered as the defining horror of the age, cited by Cicero, Sallust and every later writer, and their exclusion of the sons of the proscribed from office remained a grievance until Caesar repealed it in 49. The triumvirs revived the method in 43. Modern studies (Hinard) emphasise that the proscriptions were also a legal procedure, an attempt to define and limit vengeance that nonetheless escaped control.
set.debate: Numbers vary widely; Hinard's prosopography identifies only a fraction by name. The total number of proscribed is uncertain; Hinard's prosopography identifies only about 75 by name.

set.detail:
With both consuls of 82, Carbo and Marius the Younger, dead, Sulla wrote to the Senate suggesting that an interrex be appointed, and that the times called for a dictator, not for six months as in the old Republic, but until the state was restored. The interrex Lucius Valerius Flaccus carried a law, the lex Valeria, in late 82, appointing Sulla dictator legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae, 'for writing laws and settling the constitution', with no fixed term. The law also ratified all his past acts, gave him power of life and death over citizens, and the right to found colonies, confiscate land and make war and peace.

The dictatorship had not been used since 202. Sulla's version transformed it: his title combined the old emergency office with a constituent mandate that had parallels only in the decemvirs of 451. Cicero later called the lex Valeria the most unjust of all laws. Sulla took twenty-four lictors, as many as the kings, and appointed Flaccus as his master of horse.

Sulla held the office probably until late 81 or early 80, during which he carried his programme of reforms and continued the proscriptions.
