He then held the consulship in 80 with Metellus Pius, and declined re-election for 79. His laying down of the dictatorship and retirement to private life became one of the great puzzles of Roman history; Caesar mocked him for it, saying Sulla had not known his political ABC.

The dictatorship of Sulla was the immediate model for Caesar's dictatorships, especially his dictatorship for ten years and then perpetual dictatorship, which went further by abandoning any constituent purpose or intention of laying down the office. The dictatorship itself was abolished by Antony's law in 44.
set.debate: When Sulla laid down the dictatorship (late 81, early 80, or 79) is disputed.

set.detail:
Sulla's legislation of 82-80, carried as dictator through the assemblies, aimed to make the Senate the permanent centre of government and to remove the instruments by which tribunes and generals had challenged it. He enlarged the Senate to about 600 by enrolling some 300 equites and making the quaestorship the qualification for entry, raising the number of quaestors to twenty and so supplying the Senate automatically without censorial selection.

The tribunate was gutted: tribunes lost the right to propose laws without the Senate's prior approval, their veto was limited to protecting individuals, and holders were barred from higher office, deterring ambitious men. The cursus honorum was fixed by law: quaestor, then praetor, then consul, with minimum ages (perhaps 30, 39 and 42) and a ten-year interval before re-election to the same office. The number of praetors rose to eight, and consuls and praetors were expected to remain in Rome during their year of office and govern provinces as promagistrates afterward.

Criminal justice was reorganised into seven or more standing courts (quaestiones perpetuae) with senatorial juries: extortion, treason (lex Cornelia de maiestate, which also forbade governors to leave their provinces or make war without authorisation), murder and poisoning (de sicariis et veneficis), forgery, electoral bribery, embezzlement and violence. This was the most durable part of the reform and the foundation of Roman criminal law. He also abolished grain distributions, increased the priestly colleges to fifteen, restored co-optation in place of election, extended the pomerium, and rebuilt the Senate house.

Most of the political reforms were undone within a decade: the tribunes' powers were restored in 70 by Pompey and Crassus, and the juries were shared in the same year. The court system and the cursus rules survived. Modern scholars debate whether Sulla was a reactionary restoring an idealised past or a pragmatist reinforcing the Senate against new realities.

After his consulship of 80, Sulla retired to his estate near Puteoli, where he spent his last year writing twenty-two books of memoirs, fishing, hunting and enjoying the company of actors, among them the comedian Roscius, the mime Sorex and the female impersonator Metrobius. He was still active in local affairs, drafting a constitution for Puteoli, and on the day before his death he had the local magistrate Granius strangled in his presence for withholding funds owed for the Capitol's restoration. He died in 78, aged sixty, of a haemorrhage, apparently from liver failure; Plutarch's lurid story of a disease of lice (phthiriasis) is a literary convention for tyrants.

His funeral was the most magnificent Rome had seen. The consul Lepidus wanted to deny it; his colleague Catulus and Pompey insisted. The body was carried on a golden litter from Campania through Italy, escorted by his veterans; in Rome some 2,000 golden crowns from cities and legions accompanied it, and the ladies of Rome brought so much incense that a statue of Sulla and a lictor were modelled from it. He was the first patrician Cornelius to be cremated rather than buried, perhaps to avoid what he had done to Marius' remains. The pyre, on the Campus Martius, was lit as rain began to fall.

His tomb bore an epitaph he had written himself: no friend ever surpassed him in doing good, and no enemy in doing harm. His memoirs, dedicated to Lucullus, became a major source for Plutarch and others, ensuring his version of events, with its emphasis on Fortune and divine favour, endured.

Within months of his death, Lepidus was attacking his system, and the questions he had tried to settle by force reopened. Sulla's legacy was ambivalent: he restored the Senate's dominance but showed how to seize power with an army.
set.debate: The phthiriasis story is generally rejected as a topos; the exact date in 78 is uncertain.

set.detail:
Quintus Sertorius, a Sabine from Nursia, had served under Caepio at Arausio, swimming the Rhône to escape, under Marius against the Cimbri, where he spied in Celtic dress, and under Didius in Spain, where he lost an eye. He had joined Cinna in 87 but distanced himself from Marius' massacres. Sent as propraetor to Hither Spain in 83, he was driven out by Sulla's general Annius in 81, took to the sea with Cilician pirates, fought in Mauretania for the Moorish prince Ascalis, and captured Tingis, where he opened the supposed tomb of the giant Antaeus.

In 80 the Lusitanians, at war with Rome, invited him to lead them. He crossed the Strait with 2,600 Romans and 700 Libyans, defeated a Roman fleet off Mellaria, and joined 4,700 Lusitanians. Within a year he defeated the governor of Further Spain, Fufidius, on the Baetis, and the legates of Metellus Pius, who arrived with a proconsular army.

Sertorius combined guerrilla tactics, which the Iberians knew well, with Roman organisation. He presented himself as a legitimate Roman magistrate in exile, forming a counter-senate of 300 Roman emigrés, and as a charismatic leader to the Iberians, whose loyalty he cemented with the famous white fawn, a gift, he said, of Diana that brought him divine messages. He armed and drilled the Iberians in Roman fashion, established a school at Osca for the sons of chieftains, and restrained Roman extortion.

His return began the Sertorian War, which held two proconsular armies, including Pompey's, at bay for eight years. Modern scholars debate whether Sertorius was a Roman patriot preserving the Marian Republic in exile, as Plutarch suggests, or a warlord who aimed at an independent Spanish state; his alliance with Mithridates in 75 is cited for the latter.
set.debate: Sertorius' aims, Roman restoration or Iberian independence, remain contested.

set.detail:
In 74, after Nicomedes IV bequeathed Bithynia to Rome, Mithridates invaded with an army the sources put at 120,000 foot and 16,000 horse, defeated the consul Marcus Aurelius Cotta by land and sea at Chalcedon, and turned west to besiege Cyzicus, a wealthy city on an island joined to the mainland by bridges on the Propontis. He brought siege towers, including a hundred-cubit tower on ships, rams and a mole across the strait. The consul Lucius Licinius Lucullus, with five legions (about 30,000 men) and 2,500 cavalry, followed and occupied a hill behind the Pontic camp that controlled its supply routes, Mithridates having been persuaded by the renegade Lucius Magius, a Sertorian envoy, that the Roman soldiers would defect.

Lucullus' strategy was to starve the besiegers rather than fight. The Cyzicenes held out heroically: they burned the siege engines, cut the mole, and repaired breaches, helped by a storm that wrecked the Pontic siege towers, which the citizens attributed to Persephone, their patron goddess, whose sacrificial heifer swam across to the city. Winter came, famine and plague struck the huge Pontic army, and soldiers resorted to cannibalism. Mithridates sent his cavalry and baggage away, and Lucullus caught them at the Rhyndacus in snow, killing many and taking 15,000 prisoners and 6,000 horses.

In spring 73 Mithridates abandoned the siege. His fleet escaped by sea, but his land army retreated to Lampsacus and was cut to pieces by Lucullus at the Aesepus and Granicus. Of the invading force, Plutarch claims, perhaps 300,000 combatants and followers perished, an impossible figure that nonetheless reflects catastrophe.

Cyzicus was rewarded with freedom and territory, and its siege became a model of how to defeat a superior army by logistics. It was the turning point of the Third Mithridatic War.
set.debate: Pontic army size and losses are grossly inflated in Plutarch and Appian.

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

set.detail:
By 73 the tide in Spain had turned against Sertorius. Metellus Pius and Pompey had recovered the east coast and much of the Celtiberian interior, and Pompey's army, reinforced after his letter of 75, ground down Sertorian towns. Metellus offered a reward of 100 talents and 20,000 iugera of land for Sertorius' death. Sertorius himself, according to Plutarch, grew harsh and suspicious, surrounding himself with a Spanish bodyguard, punishing the boys of the Osca school and alienating Roman officers.

The plot was led by Marcus Perperna Veiento, the aristocratic former Lepidan who had joined Sertorius in 77 with his own army and resented his subordinate role. At a banquet at Osca, arranged by Perperna to celebrate a fictitious victory, the conspirators behaved with deliberate indecency to provoke Sertorius; when he turned away on his couch in disgust, Perperna gave a signal by dropping a cup, and they stabbed him to death. The Iberian devoti who had sworn to die with him killed themselves.

Perperna took command, but his army distrusted him. In 72 Pompey lured him into an ambush and destroyed his forces. Perperna offered Pompey Sertorius' correspondence, which supposedly incriminated leading Roman senators; Pompey burned the letters unread and executed him, an act widely praised as statesmanlike. The last Sertorian towns, Uxama, Clunia and Calagurris, fell soon after, Calagurris only after famine drove its people to cannibalism.

Sertorius' career fascinated ancient writers. Plutarch paired him with Eumenes of Cardia, another foreign general fighting for a cause in exile. Sallust, whose Histories gave him a central role, presented him as a talented Roman who deserved better. Spain was pacified by Pompey, who settled his veterans and rewarded supporters with citizenship, building a Pompeian clientele there that would fight for his sons a generation later.
set.debate: Date of the murder 73 or 72. Date (73 or 72) and place (Osca) of the murder are not certain.

scholarship: Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)

set.detail:
In 73 some seventy-eight gladiators broke out of the training school of Gnaeus Lentulus Batiatus at Capua, armed with kitchen knives and spits, seized a wagon carrying gladiatorial weapons and made for Mount Vesuvius, then a wooded mountain with a flat crater top. They chose three leaders: the Thracian Spartacus, who had served in the Roman army as an auxiliary before deserting, and the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus. Plutarch says Spartacus' wife, a prophetess of Dionysus, had foretold his greatness when a snake coiled round his face as he slept.

Rome treated the outbreak as a police matter. The praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber, with 3,000 hastily raised men, besieged the fugitives on Vesuvius; Spartacus' men climbed down a cliff on ladders woven from wild vines and attacked Glaber's camp from behind, routing it. A second praetor, Publius Varinius, was defeated in several encounters, losing his lictors and horse. Slaves, herdsmen and free rural poor joined in thousands, and the movement spread through Campania, Lucania and Apulia, sacking towns such as Nola, Nuceria, Thurii and Metapontum.

The ancient sources disagree on Spartacus' aims. Plutarch portrays him as wanting to lead his followers home across the Alps; Appian says he sought to march on Rome; Sallust's fragments show internal disputes between Spartacus and the Gauls who wanted to plunder Italy. Modern interpretations range from the Marxist image of a revolutionary seeking to abolish slavery, influential in the twentieth century, to the view (Shaw, Strauss) that the revolt had no programme beyond survival and plunder.

The revolt grew because Rome's best armies were in Spain under Pompey and in Asia under Lucullus. By 72 Spartacus commanded perhaps 70,000 or more, and the third servile war had become a major military crisis in Italy.
set.debate: Spartacus' goals and the social composition of his army (slaves only, or free poor as well) are debated.

scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
